questions.q: What is the fundamental trade-off data compression makes, according to this lesson?
options: It spends more CPU to compress/decompress data in exchange for less I/O and better buffer-pool efficiency
It spends more memory in exchange for faster network transfer
It has no real trade-off — it is always strictly better
It spends disk space in exchange for CPU savings
questions.explain: Smaller pages reduce I/O, but every read and write now pays a CPU cost to decompress and recompress the data.

questions.q: What does PAGE compression do that ROW compression does not?
options: It adds prefix compression and dictionary compression at the page level, on top of everything ROW compression does
It only works on partitioned tables
It compresses the transaction log instead of the data
It removes the need for indexes
questions.explain: PAGE compression includes ROW compression's byte-trimming plus prefix compression (shared leading patterns) and dictionary compression (repeated page-level values), at a higher CPU cost per operation.

Immediately applies PAGE compression to the table

questions.explain: It's a planning tool — you use it to decide whether the space savings are worth the CPU cost before you actually commit to a rebuild.

questions.q: According to this lesson's guidance table, which workload is the best candidate for PAGE compression?
options: A large, mostly-read, historical/cold table on an I/O-bound server
A small, frequently-updated hot table on a CPU-constrained OLTP server
Any table, regardless of access pattern or server load
Only tables with fewer than 100 rows
questions.explain: Cold, read-heavy tables get the I/O and space win from PAGE compression without paying a heavy recurring CPU cost, since they aren't being decompressed/recompressed on constant writes.

questions.q: Why might compression make performance worse on a database that is already CPU-bound?
options: Because every read and write now spends additional CPU cycles decompressing and recompressing data, on a resource that's already the bottleneck
Because compression always corrupts data on CPU-bound servers
Because compressed tables can no longer be queried at all
Because compression disables all indexes automatically
questions.explain: Compression trades I/O for CPU. If CPU is already the scarce resource, adding more CPU work on every operation can make the real bottleneck worse instead of better.
